#remove the data with more than 80% missing values
```{r}
missing_metadata %>%
filter(Missing_Percentage > 80)

vars_remove <- missing_metadata %>%
filter(Missing_Percentage > 80) %>%
pull(Variable)
sample_metadata_filtered <- sample_metadata %>%
select(-any_of(vars_remove))
```

Several variables contained extensive missingness (>80%), suggesting that these measurements were only available for a subset of participants rather than being randomly missing. Such variables were considered unsuitable for analyses involving the full cohort.

counting the missing values (NAs) in age group, biological sex and CMV status to check how complete the metadata is. Samples with a missing value in these columns would be dropped from any model that uses them, so this tells you how many samples you can actually analyze.

conclusion: There are no missing values in any of the three columns. Age group, biological sex and CMV status are filled in for every sample, so we can use them in our analysis without losing any samples to missing data.

step 5: filter for duplicates 
#check if no duplicate protein measurements have occurred under different IDs:
```{r}
pairs_df <- protein_annotation %>%
  filter(!is.na(same_assay_as)) %>%
  arrange(n_missing) %>%
  distinct(olink_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
nrow(pairs_df)
```
We have found 9 duplicates.
these have to be deleted.
```{r}
proteins_npx_clean <- proteins_npx_raw
for (i in seq_len(nrow(pairs_df))) {
  new_col <- pairs_df$protein[i]
  old_col <- pairs_df$same_assay_as[i]
  
  proteins_npx_clean[[new_col]] <- coalesce(proteins_npx_clean[[new_col]], proteins_npx_clean[[old_col]])
  proteins_npx_clean[[old_col]] <- NULL
}
```
```{r}
# 3.Also update protein_annotation (1472 unique proteins)
protein_annotation_clean <- protein_annotation %>%
  filter(!protein %in% pairs_df$same_assay_as) %>%
  mutate(
    n_missing = if_else(protein %in% pairs_df$protein, 0L, n_missing),
    pct_missing = if_else(protein %in% pairs_df$protein, 0.0, pct_missing)
  )
```
```{r}
# Check if the 9 joined proteins are no longer missing
colSums(is.na(proteins_npx_clean[pairs_df$protein]))
```

part 2 

**research question:**
Does the change in plasma CXCL13 concentration between day 0 and day 7 after seasonal influenza vaccination differ between young and older adults, independently of biological sex, CMV status and batch?

**Hypothese:**
* **H0:** The change in plasma CXCL13 levels from day 0 to day 7 does not differ between young and older adults after adjustment ($\beta_{\text{visit} \times \text{ageGroup}} = 0$).
* **H1:** The change in plasma CXCL13 levels from day 0 to day 7 differs significantly between young and older adults after adjustment ($\beta_{\text{visit} \times \text{ageGroup}} \neq 0$).

**Variables:**
* **Outcome (afhankelijke variabele):** `CXCL13` (continue NPX-waarde op $\log_2$-schaal).
* **Hoofdpredictoren (interactie):** `sample.visit` (discreet/binair na filtering: Day 0 vs. Day 7) en `subject.ageGroup` (binair categorisch: Young Adult vs. Older Adult).
* **Covariaten (confounders) & random effect:** `subject.biologicalSex` (Female vs. Male), `cmv_status` (Negative vs. Positive), `olink_batch_id` (categorisch, meerdere levels) en een random intercept voor `subject.subjectGuid` (om te corrigeren voor herhaalde metingen binnen dezelfde donor).



step 1: filtering 
we will analyse the cohort flu Year 1 day O in comparison to Flu Year Day 7 
select this data
```{r}
analysis_data <- subset(
  data,
  sample.visitName %in% c(
    "Flu Year 1 Day 0",
    "Flu Year 1 Day 7"
  )
)
```


```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
# convert measurement moments to categorical variable. This ensures that R treats the visit as a category, and not as a numerical value. 
#reason => Visits are labels for time points, not quantities. If R treats them as numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 3), a model assumes a straight-line effect and that the gaps between visits are equal. As a category, each visit gets its own estimate, so differences between specific visits can be tested without those assumptions.
analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    visit = factor(sample.visitName,
                   levels = c("Flu Year 1 Day 0", "Flu Year 1 Day 7"),
                   labels = c("Day 0", "Day 7")),
    #The code determines the order of the categories.
    age_group = factor(subject.ageGroup, levels = c("Young Adult", "Older Adult")),
    #Convert other variables into factors because they must be treated as groups or categories in the statistical       model, and not as numerical values.
    sex = factor(subject.biologicalSex),
    cmv_status = factor(cmv_status),
    batch = factor(olink_batch_id),
    donor = factor(subject.subjectGuid)
    #filter = the code removes all rows in which at least one of these variables is missing:
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(CXCL13),
    !is.na(visit),
    !is.na(age_group),
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(cmv_status),
    !is.na(batch),
    !is.na(donor)
  )

# Controleer de aantallen per bezoek en leeftijdsgroep= je controleert hoeveel observaties er per visit en leeftijdsgroep overblijven.
table(Visit = analysis_data$visit, AgeGroup = analysis_data$age_group)
```



# Fit the linear mixed-effects model to analysis_data
Because your data have repeated measures: the same subject is measured at several visits (you counted unique subject.subjectGuid earlier). Measurements from the same person are not independent, so an ordinary linear model or t-test would treat them as independent and make the SE too small (pseudo-replication).
```{r}
model_protein_cxcl13 <- lmer(
  CXCL13 ~ visit * age_group + sex + cmv_status + batch + (1 | donor),
  data = analysis_data
)
summary(model_protein_cxcl13)
```

Conclusion:
The linear mixed-effects model, including donor as a random intercept, showed substantial inter-individual variability, with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.606. No significant main effect of visit (Day 7 vs. Day 0; β = -0.006, p = 0.946) or age group (Older Adults vs. Younger Adults; β = -0.220, p = 0.165) was observed. Furthermore, no significant interaction between visit and age group was detected (β = -0.095, p = 0.472), indicating no evidence of differential changes over time between the two age groups. Significant effects were observed for sex (β = -0.347, p = 0.012) and batch 20212223 (β = -0.901, p = 0.010).

step 2 further checks:
1) Adjusted CXCL13 levels across visits by age group
reason => Model-estimated mean CXCL13 (NPX) at each visit for each age group, adjusted for the other model variables and the repeated measures per subject. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals.
```{r}
library(emmeans)
emm <- emmeans(model_protein_cxcl13, ~ visit * age_group)
emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm)
ggplot(emm_df,
       aes(x = visit,
           y = emmean,
           color = age_group,
           group = age_group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower.CL,
                    ymax = upper.CL),
                width = 0.1) +
  labs(
    x = "Visit",
    y = "Adjusted CXCL13 (NPX)",
    color = "Age group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```
conclusion: We see that young adults have higher values on both measurement days; there is no real difference between the two days.
Older adults have clearly lower values but do show a decrease on day 0 compared to day 7.
#estimate marginal means (EMMs) 
= These are the average CXCL13 values per group, adjusted for sex, cmv_status, and batch.
= The adjusted averages show what each group's mean would be if the groups were comparable on sex, CMV status and batch.
```{r}
emm
```
conclusion:
Adjusted for sex, CMV status and batch, CXCL13 levels were stable between Day 0 and Day 7 in young adults (0.33 vs 0.33 NPX) and showed only a small decrease in older adults (0.11 vs 0.01 NPX). Older adults tended to have lower CXCL13 than young adults at both visits, but the 95% confidence intervals overlapped substantially, so these data do not show a clear difference between age groups or visits. Formal contrasts or an interaction test are needed to confirm this.

```{r}
#compares all the estimated means with each other, two at a time (pairwise contrasts).
pairs(emmeans(model_protein_cxcl13,
~ age_group | visit))
```
conclusion
After adjusting for sex, CMV status and batch, young adults had higher CXCL13 than older adults at Day 7 (difference 0.32 NPX, p = 0.045), but not at Day 0 (difference 0.22 NPX, p = 0.165). The Day 7 difference is borderline and does not remain significant after correcting for the two comparisons, so the evidence for an age difference in CXCL13 is weak and should be confirmed in further data.
#Question: Does CXCL13 change over time, and does this happen in both groups?
```{r}
pairs(emmeans(model_protein_cxcl13,
              ~ visit | age_group))
```
CXCL13 levels did not change significantly between Day 0 and Day 7 in either young or older adults. Furthermore, no significant visit-by-age group interaction was observed, indicating that the temporal evolution of CXCL13 did not differ significantly between age groups. A post-hoc comparison showed higher CXCL13 levels in young adults compared with older adults at Day 7 (p = 0.045), but this isolated finding should be interpreted with caution given the absence of a significant overall age-group effect or interaction.

Checking model assumptions
Linearity and homoscedasticity (Residues versus Fitted )
= Linearity: Is the relationship between the predicted values ​​and the outcome variable sufficiently linear?
= Homoscedasticity: Does the spread of the residuals remain approximately the same over the entire range of the predicted values?
```{r}
plot(fitted(model_protein_cxcl13), resid(model_protein_cxcl13),
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "pink")
```
conclusion:Conclusion: The graph of residuals versus predicted values ​​shows that the residuals are largely centered around zero without pronounced nonlinearity, accompanied by slight heteroscedasticity and a few increased positive residuals at higher predicted values; given the sample size ($n = 184$), these small deviations do not substantially compromise the inference of the model.

# 2. Normality of the residues:
The normality of the residuals was assessed using a Q-Q plot. The residuals approximately followed the theoretical normal distribution, suggesting that the assumption of normally distributed residuals was reasonably met.
```{r}
qqnorm(resid(model_protein_cxcl13), main = "Q-Q Residuals")
qqline(resid(model_protein_cxcl13), col = "red")
```
The residues largely follow the normal processing of the reference, with only a small part in the added and other steps; this does not constitute a substantial objection to the validity of the model.


# 3. Normality of random intercepts (donor)
You check whether the random intercepts of the 92 donors are approximately normally distributed.
```{r}
qqnorm(unlist(ranef(model_protein_cxcl13)$donor), main = "Q-Q Random Intercepts")
qqline(unlist(ranef(model_protein_cxcl13)$donor), col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
conclusion: The normality of the random effects was assessed using a Q-Q plot of the donor-specific random intercepts. The random intercepts approximately followed a normal distribution, suggesting that the normality assumption for the random effects was reasonably met.

visualizeren:
paired-plot
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Haal de data uit het mixed model
data_cxcl13 <- model.frame(model_protein_cxcl13)

# Maak de paired plot
ggplot(data_cxcl13,
       aes(x = visit,
           y = CXCL13,
           group = donor,
           color = age_group)) +

  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.5) +

  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.75) +

  stat_summary(
    aes(group = age_group),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    linewidth = 1.3
  ) +

  stat_summary(
    aes(group = age_group),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "CXCL13 concentrations before and after influenza vaccination",
    x = "Visit",
    y = "CXCL13",
    color = "Age group"
  ) +

  theme_classic()
```
conclusie: The individual profiles in large groups show latency in CXCL13 values ​​from day 0 to day 7, remaining largely stable for both young adults and the elderly with sufficient parallel trajectories, whereas it exhibits a significantly different existence between individual donors.

report:
```{r}
summary(model_protein_cxcl13)
```
```{r}
confint(model_protein_cxcl13)
```
No significant visit-by-age group interaction was observed for CXCL13 (β = -0.095, 95% CI [-0.353, 0.163], p = 0.472), indicating that the change in CXCL13 concentrations between Day 0 and Day 7 did not differ significantly between young and older adults.
